episodes: Ep 234: Webb has imaged a giant planet seven point six times Jupiter's mass just twelve light-years away.
Ep 233: Astronomers have found evidence of a Jupiter-mass exosatellite orbiting a brown dwarf in the CD-35 2722 system.
Ep 232: White dwarfs can appear yellow, pink or purple when trace elements in their dense atmospheres filter the light they emit.
Ep 231: Europe will begin independent cargo deliveries to the lunar surface from 2030 with its new Argonaut lander.
Ep 230: Expansion may place entire galaxies permanently beyond any telescope's reach.
Ep 229: Simulations show merging neutron stars can boost their magnetic fields more than 300 times in one millisecond.
Ep 228: A European service station on the Moon will keep experiments running for years by storing solar power for the two-week lunar night.
Ep 227: A two-million-light-year radio structure shaped like a treble clef was re-energized by a galaxy cluster collision.
Ep 226: Four Artemis II astronauts accepted the Stephen Hawking Medal for turning their lunar flight into a shared human experience.
Ep 225: Seven billion light-years away, a supercluster holding more than two quadrillion solar masses may show whether dark matter particles interact with one another.
Ep 224: Detailed maps of young lunar faults now give the clearest measure yet of how much the moon has contracted while cooling.
Ep 223: Perseverance has driven farther on Mars than any rover before it thanks to its AutoNav hazard system.
Ep 222: Perseverance rover just added another 91 meters to its Mars record in one day, pushing the total distance past prior benchmarks.
Ep 221: New helium measurements are confirming the exact mix forged in the universe's first minutes.
Ep 220: European companies will test lunar rovers inside new Italian simulation facilities.
Ep 219: Astronomers have fresh clues about the irregular dimming of Tabby's Star that once hinted at alien structures.
Ep 218: A sharp mosaic from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter shows the Moon's farside has a thicker crust that prevents dark maria from forming.
Ep 217: A high school student has identified three dwarf galaxies whose star formation patterns may resolve a long-standing puzzle about isolated systems.
Ep 216: A radio galaxy from nearly twelve point five billion years ago has been confirmed as one of the most powerful ever detected.
Ep 215: Sophie Adenot and her Crew-12 crewmates undocked from the International Space Station today after nearly eight months aboard.
Ep 214: SpaceX Crew Dragon Grace reached the International Space Station in seven hours and fifty-five minutes, the fastest U.S. spacecraft transit on record.
Ep 213: Tidal streams around the Sombrero galaxy show it grew through repeated mergers thirty million light years away.
Ep 212: Starlink is beta testing a program allowing property owners to earn passive income by sharing satellite internet with nearby users.
Ep 211: SpaceX completed three Falcon launches, four first stage landings, and a Dragon docking to the station in under thirteen hours.
Ep 211: A double neutron star system with the lowest total mass recorded so far has been identified by radio observations.
Ep 210: Researchers now estimate Mars north pole ice contains only three percent dust by mass instead of the prior twenty five percent figure.
Ep 209: Webb telescope image of galaxy cluster MACS J0454.1-0300 shows hundreds more galaxies than Hubble captured in 2014.
Ep 208: NASA will pay Boeing three hundred fifty nine million dollars to return Starliner to flight and certify a new rocket.
Ep 207: A new map reveals hundreds of previously unknown valleys beneath Greenland's vast ice sheet.
Ep 206: JWST data shows Chariklo's inner ring grew over fifty percent denser while its outer ring thinned by sixty percent.
Ep 205: The LINK spacecraft reentered over the South Pacific after failing its rescue mission for the SWIFT observatory.
Ep 204: Côte d'Ivoire becomes the seventy fifth nation to sign the Artemis Accords, expanding international commitments for lunar operations.
Ep 203: Chinese spaceplane executed a rerendezvous with its subsat on September tenth and a recapture on September thirteenth.
Ep 202: McGetchin crater on the Moon gets its name in today's astronomy picture of the day.
Ep 201: Astronomers have detected the first direct radio signals from an exoplanet, opening a new window on distant worlds.
Ep 200: New research suggests Venus may have devoured its own moon, explaining its current lack of satellites.
Ep 199: Astronaut Tim Peake revealed the one everyday item he most missed during his time aboard the International Space Station.
Ep 198: Astronomers are pushing back against a plan to launch mirrors that would brighten the night sky from orbit.
Ep 197: Astronomers have discovered the youngest known exoplanet, a baby world still forming at just one million years old.
Ep 196: Liquid nitrogen appears to have flowed across Pluto, captured in fresh images from a spacecraft that left Earth in 2006.
Ep 195: An invisible mass equivalent to tens of thousands of galaxies is dragging the Milky Way and its neighbors across space at 600 km/s.
Ep 194: An amateur map scout hunting Quebec campsites instead found a hidden impact crater from space.
Ep 193: New analysis shows the moon's polar water deposits fall far short of what would be needed to sustain cities or heavy industry on the lunar surface.
Ep 192: A fresh catalog of nearly 3,000 supernovae is already testing long-held ideas about what drives the universe’s expansion.
Ep 191: A distant exoplanet hosts winds racing at 5400 mph, far faster than anything in our solar system.
Ep 190: A new X-ray catalog just doubled the known high-energy sources across the sky.
Ep 189: UK astronomers have traced the third known interstellar object back to its likely birthplace in another star system.
Ep 188: Telescopes reveal the most distant galaxy supercluster seed yet, showing how the cosmic web first took shape.
Ep 187: Hubble captures a striking decagon of clouds locked around Saturn’s south pole.
Ep 186: The Sun's vast magnetic boundary just came into sharper focus from a third of Earth's distance.
Ep 185: A private German rocket just became the first to reach orbit from continental Europe, opening a new chapter for the continent's launch independence.
Ep 184: Radio astronomers have captured hydrogen signals from when the universe was billions of years younger, giving a fresh window into its early structure.
Ep 183: A distant icy body is caught mid-transformation into an active comet, revealing a key stage in how these objects evolve.
Ep 182: Sierra Space has locked in the first payloads for Dream Chaser’s debut flight, marking a concrete step for commercial cargo to orbit.
Ep 181: A single particle interaction recorded a mile underground has physicists rethinking how dark matter might finally reveal itself.
Ep 180: Blue Origin is building a 120,000-square-foot facility to handle the large payloads its future missions will require.
Ep 179: ESA's JUICE probe will swing past a dark, untouched Jovian moon in 2031 that may preserve the solar system's original building blocks.
Ep 178: Researchers melted diamond under crushing pressure to recreate the weather inside ice giants like Neptune.
Ep 177: A Canadian university lab is teaming up with the Canadian Space Agency to explore how living systems could manufacture materials beyond Earth.
Ep 176: A European weather satellite has reached its transfer orbit and is confirmed healthy after an Ariane 6 launch.
Ep 175: A failed private rescue leaves NASA's Swift telescope on course for an uncontrolled return to Earth.
Ep 174: Europe just signed its first contracts to grow independent launch capability while Venus clouds keep hiding an unknown absorber that has puzzled scientists for a century.
Ep 173: A new vest design could cut cancer risk for astronauts heading beyond Earth’s protective field.
Ep 172: After an eight-year trek, a joint ESA-JAXA spacecraft is about to become the third to orbit Mercury and the first to deliver two probes at once.
Ep 171: A fleet of seventeen spacecraft has shown that solar eruptions stretch across a far larger volume of the solar system than models predicted.
Ep 170: Earth's shadow will soon swallow 96 percent of the Moon, giving the Americas a front-row seat to a deep partial eclipse.
Ep 169: A suitcase-sized satellite on the Moon’s far side could finally listen to the universe’s first 150 million years of silence.
Ep 169: A lab experiment has now shown that intense magnetic fields around other stars can completely shut down the massive plasma eruptions we see from the Sun.
Ep 168: Multiple observatories have combined forces to reveal the Tarantula Nebula’s turbulent star birth in unprecedented color and detail.
Ep 168: Europe's Mars Express has returned the sharpest flyover yet of the crater that stranded Mark Watney in fiction.
Ep 167: A satellite built to measure photosynthesis from orbit just received its final fuel load ahead of a September launch.
Ep 166: A star has been clocked orbiting the Milky Way's central black hole at 25,000 km/s, closer than any previously observed.
Ep 165: Gaia and Hubble have traced the Milky Way’s first major collision to a dwarf galaxy swallowed nearly 12 billion years ago.
Ep 164: Spherical robots may soon explore hidden caves on Saturn’s moon Titan in search of subsurface oceans.
Ep 163: Astronomers may have been reading the wrong spin on distant worlds because thick atmospheres whip around far faster than the planet beneath.
Ep 162: Orbital mirrors could flood the night sky with light brighter than the full Moon across tens of kilometres.
Ep 161: A rare star stream outside the Milky Way just gave astronomers a new way to weigh dark matter in distant galaxies.
Ep 160: A new X-ray catalog of two million sources shows galaxy cluster outskirts hotter and cleaner than models predicted.
Ep 159: A star near our galaxy’s central black hole is still forming dust and water despite extreme radiation.
Ep 158: Webb reveals dust and water forming right next to the Milky Way’s central black hole, defying expectations for such a harsh environment.
Ep 157: Astronomers watched a lone black hole shred a star, revealing how these wanderers reshape galaxies.
Ep 156: A self-driving rover on Mars has already shattered every distance record set by earlier missions.
Ep 155: A gravitational arc candidate at redshift near 4.4 has appeared in public James Webb data, revealing structure from when the universe was less than 1.5 billion years old.
Ep 154: A trillion-mile gas streamer is tilting the planet-forming disk around a young triple star, showing how material from outside can reshape entire systems.
Ep 153: A Falcon 9 upper stage slammed into the Moon after drifting for a year, giving orbiters a live view of the impact flash and plume.
Ep 152: Webb’s pinhole mask is letting astronomers resolve details on Io and young stars that ordinary imaging cannot reach.
Ep 151: Astronomers have now searched far more of the Milky Way for alien signals than anyone realized.
Ep 150: A spent Falcon 9 stage is heading for a lunar impact this week that orbiters will track in real time.
Ep 149: A new Chinese lunar mission is drawing interest from an entire continent while NASA’s rover uncovers strange honeycomb patterns etched into Martian rock.
Ep 148: Astronomers have detected the first exomoon, opening a new window on how satellites form beyond our solar system.
Ep 147: Venus will dominate evening skies this August while Mercury and Jupiter form a tight dawn pairing.
Ep 146: Webb is tracing how the universe’s earliest mysterious red objects may have simply grown into the galaxies around us today.
Ep 146: Astronomers may have found the first confirmed exomoon, and its size and orbit challenge every formation model we have.
Ep 145: Radio telescopes have tracked space debris for the first time by listening for its own faint signals.
Ep 144: A seed that circled the Moon now grows into a living tree in the middle of Manhattan.
Ep 143: Three astronauts are heading home after 241 days in orbit while Juno reaches its closest approach to Earth.
Ep 142: Astronomers report the first strong evidence for an exomoon orbiting a planet 73 light-years away.
Ep 141: Hubble has found the first “missing” black hole inside a famous star cluster by combining two decades of data with new infrared views.
Ep 140: A candidate Jupiter-sized moon orbiting far beyond our solar system is forcing astronomers to redraw the line between planets and moons.
Ep 139: A European spacecraft just cleared its final major test before hunting Earth-like worlds around Sun-like stars.
Ep 138: Astronomers have watched a distant galaxy's central black hole erupt for the first time in real time after two prior outbursts went unseen until they faded.
Ep 137: Fifty years after Viking 1 touched down on Mars, new missions are shifting focus from the surface to the thin air above the Red Planet.
Ep 136: NASA's Psyche spacecraft just used Mars as a gravitational slingshot, returning a rich dataset that will sharpen its approach to a metal world never visited before.
Ep 135: A private Indian rocket just reached orbit on its first try while a NASA probe wakes up billions of miles out.
Ep 134: Astronomers report signs of an atmosphere on a rocky world in the habitable zone 48 light-years away, a first for planets of its kind.
Ep 133: Astronomers have directly imaged a third giant planet in the Beta Pictoris system by spotting its carbon monoxide signature with JWST.
Ep 132: China's Tianwen-2 probe has reached a near-Earth asteroid after a billion-kilometre chase, raising the possibility that the target is a long-lost lunar fragment.
Ep 131: Four new NASA missions will help turn the Moon into a permanent base while another rover just ran a full marathon on Mars.
Ep 130: A Chinese probe has reached a quasi-moon while JWST reveals a hot Jupiter with violently different day and night sides.
Ep 129: UN records now let anyone track satellite registrations that official sites still hide.
Ep 128: Japan just completed the first test flight of an experimental reusable rocket, landing it safely after launch.
Ep 127: A Chinese rocket just became only the second booster ever recovered after an orbital launch, landing on a barge after sending its payload skyward.
Ep 126: A Falcon 9 booster has now completed its 36th flight and landing, carrying 29 more Starlink satellites into orbit.
Ep 125: A total solar eclipse will turn day to night across northern Spain next month as the Moon fully covers the Sun.
Ep 124: Euclid telescope has found the two oldest quasars known, their light crossing more than 13 billion years to reach us.
Ep 123: An asteroid set for a once-in-a-millennium Earth flyby could be seen by ninety percent of the world's population.
Ep 122: Astronomers just found giant planets lighter than cotton candy, forcing a rethink of how worlds assemble.
Ep 121: A robotic spacecraft just launched to nudge a long-running NASA observatory back into a stable orbit.
Ep 120: A planet 25 light-years away shows signs it could support liquid water on its surface.
Ep 119: A Jupiter-sized world lighter than cotton candy shows that giant planets can form with almost no solid core.
Ep 118: NASA is weighing whether to send a spare Mars rover to the Moon while awarding nearly $600 million in new lunar lander contracts.
Ep 117: NASA is launching a robot to lift its aging Swift telescope before atmospheric drag pulls it down.
Ep 116: Supermassive black holes keep flinging radio-emitting material into space years after swallowing a star, showing their appetites stay active long after the initial feast.
Ep 115: The week's biggest developments, pulled together — what actually moved, why it matters, and what to watch next.
Ep 114: Mars is gliding past the Pleiades star cluster in the early-morning sky, offering a rare close pairing visible before sunrise.
Ep 113: After eight years of continuous thrust, BepiColombo has powered down its engines for the final coast toward Mercury.
Ep 112: Astronomers have captured the first “fingerprints” of a black hole’s event horizon, the boundary where nothing escapes.
Ep 111: An asteroid impact that ended the dinosaurs also sustained underground conditions for life eight million years longer than earlier estimates.
Ep 110: An interstellar comet that passed the Sun last year may be nearly three times older than our Solar System and formed in a stellar system nothing like our own.
Ep 109: NASA’s next flagship observatory has reached Florida for final checks before an August launch on a Falcon Heavy.
Ep 108: The week's biggest developments, pulled together — what actually moved, why it matters, and what to watch next.
Ep 107: JWST has imaged a galaxy cluster so massive and concentrated that it formed when such structures were not expected to exist yet.
Ep 106: A distant exoplanet once nicknamed the Pink Planet turns out to host salty clouds detectable only through infrared observations that pierce its thick atmosphere.
Ep 105: An upgraded Ariane 6 just lofted Europe’s heaviest payload ever, 36 Amazon satellites riding on boosters carrying 14 extra tonnes of propellant each.
Ep 104: Chandra spots possible supernova remains surprisingly close to the Milky Way’s central black hole.
Ep 103: China's Tianwen-2 probe is executing a string of fine burns to reach its target asteroid next month.
Ep 102: Tiny red dots scattered across the early universe have turned out to be black holes cloaked in dense gas.
Ep 101: The week's biggest developments, pulled together — what actually moved, why it matters, and what to watch next.
